wsgnstat: the wrapped skew generalised normal distribution

Source: vignettes/wsgnstat.Rmd
wsgnstat.Rmd
library(wsgnstat)

The law and its parameters

On the line, the skew generalised normal distribution has the two-piece exponential-power density

f(x)=cexp⁡{−(λ±|x−μ|σ)β},c=1σ(1/λ1+1/λ2)Γ(1+1/β), f(x) = c \, \exp\!\left\{-\left(\frac{\lambda_{\pm} |x - \mu|}{\sigma}\right)^{\beta}\right\}, \qquad c = \frac{1}{\sigma \, (1/\lambda_1 + 1/\lambda_2) \, \Gamma(1 + 1/\beta)},

with λ1\lambda_1 to the right of the location μ\mu and λ2\lambda_2 to its left. It is the scale mixture of a uniform variable and a generalised gamma variable, which is how rsgn() draws from it. The shape β>0\beta > 0 governs the tails (β=2\beta = 2 is Gaussian, β=1\beta = 1 Laplace-like, smaller values heavier), and the pair (λ1,λ2)(\lambda_1, \lambda_2) the asymmetry: the mass to the left of μ\mu is λ1/(λ1+λ2)\lambda_1 / (\lambda_1 + \lambda_2).

Wrapping onto the circle sums the line density over all turns, fW(θ)=∑kf(θ+2πk)f_W(\theta) = \sum_k f(\theta + 2\pi k). On the circle the package uses the identified parameterisation λ1=λ\lambda_1 = \lambda, λ2=1−λ\lambda_2 = 1 - \lambda and σ=λ(1−λ)\sigma = \sqrt{\lambda (1 - \lambda)}, so the circular law has three parameters: the location mu, the tail parameter beta and the skewness lam, with lam = 0.5 symmetric. For a skew law mu is the junction of the two pieces, not the mean direction.

th <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 721)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (b in c(0.8, 1.5, 3)) {
  plot(th, dwsgn(th, mu = pi, beta = b, lam = 0.5), type = "l", ylim = c(0, 1.2),
       xlab = "angle (radians)", ylab = "density", main = paste("beta =", b))
  lines(th, dwsgn(th, mu = pi, beta = b, lam = 0.25), lty = 2)
}

Wrapped densities for three tail parameters, symmetric (solid) and skew (dashed). 

par(op)

Density, distribution function, quantiles and random generation

The four functions follow R’s usual naming. The distribution function is measured anticlockwise from angle zero and is computed exactly, as a sum over turns of incomplete gamma functions, so it needs no numerical quadrature; the quantile function inverts it.

mu <- 1
beta <- 1.5
lam <- 0.3
dwsgn(c(0.5, 1, 2), mu, beta, lam)
#> [1] 0.2607334 0.5077476 0.2989011
pwsgn(c(0.5, 1, 2), mu, beta, lam)
#> [1] 0.07806267 0.27633042 0.69219129
qwsgn(c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), mu, beta, lam)
#> [1] 0.5779239 1.4711739 3.1037257

The distribution function agrees with direct numerical integration of the density, and the density integrates to one over the circle:

c(pwsgn = pwsgn(2, mu, beta, lam),
  integrate = integrate(dwsgn, 0, 2, mu = mu, beta = beta, lam = lam)$value,
  total = integrate(dwsgn, 0, 2 * pi, mu = mu, beta = beta, lam = lam)$value)
#>     pwsgn integrate     total 
#> 0.6921913 0.6921913 0.9999999

Draws in the identified parameterisation come from rwsgn(); rsgn() draws on the line, and wraps if asked, for any (σ,λ1,λ2)(\sigma, \lambda_1, \lambda_2).

set.seed(1)
x <- rwsgn(5000, mu, beta, lam)
hist(x, breaks = seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 49), freq = FALSE, main = "",
     xlab = "angle (radians)")
curve(dwsgn(x, mu, beta, lam), 0, 2 * pi, add = TRUE, lwd = 2)

A sample of 5000 draws with the wrapped density overlaid.

A Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between the sample and the exact distribution function confirms the agreement:

u <- sort(pwsgn(x, mu, beta, lam))
n <- length(u)
c(KS = max(pmax((1:n) / n - u, u - (0:(n - 1)) / n)), five_per_cent_critical = 1.358 / sqrt(n))
#>                     KS five_per_cent_critical 
#>             0.01316301             0.01920502

Reductions to known circular laws

At β=2\beta = 2 the line law is the two-piece (split) normal, so the circular law is the wrapped split normal; with lam = 0.5 as well, σ=1/2\sigma = 1/2 and the rate is one on both sides, so the line law is N(0,1/2)N(0, 1/2) and the circular law is the wrapped normal with σ=1/2\sigma = 1/\sqrt{2}. Both reductions can be checked against densities built directly from dnorm():

tt <- c(0.5, 2, 4.5)
k <- -60:60
wrapped_normal <- vapply(tt, function(t) sum(dnorm(t + 2 * pi * k, 0, sqrt(1 / 2))), 0)
rbind(wsgnstat = dwsgn(tt, mu = 0, beta = 2, lam = 0.5), wrapped_normal = wrapped_normal)
#>                     [,1]      [,2]       [,3]
#> wsgnstat       0.4393913 0.0103335 0.02346806
#> wrapped_normal 0.4393913 0.0103335 0.02346806

## wrapped split normal: standard deviation sigma / (sqrt(2) lam) on the right of mu and
## sigma / (sqrt(2) (1 - lam)) on the left, with left mass lam
l <- 0.3
s <- sqrt(l * (1 - l))
split_normal <- function(x) {
  sr <- s / (sqrt(2) * l)
  sl <- s / (sqrt(2) * (1 - l))
  ifelse(x >= 0, 2 * (1 - l) * dnorm(x, 0, sr), 2 * l * dnorm(x, 0, sl))
}
wrapped_split <- vapply(tt, function(t) sum(split_normal(t + 2 * pi * k)), 0)
rbind(wsgnstat = dwsgn(tt, mu = 0, beta = 2, lam = l), wrapped_split_normal = wrapped_split)
#>                           [,1]       [,2]         [,3]
#> wsgnstat             0.4645507 0.09312363 0.0003979992
#> wrapped_split_normal 0.4645507 0.09312363 0.0003979992

The trigonometric moments of the wrapped normal are exp⁡(−p2σ2/2)=exp⁡(−p2/4)\exp(-p^2 \sigma^2 / 2) = \exp(-p^2/4), and the engine reproduces them through its characteristic function:

tm <- trig_moments(4, mu = 0, beta = 2, lam = 0.5)
rbind(engine = tm$A, closed_form = exp(-(1:4)^2 / 4))
#>                  [,1]      [,2]      [,3]       [,4]
#> engine      0.7788008 0.3678794 0.1053992 0.01831564
#> closed_form 0.7788008 0.3678794 0.1053992 0.01831564

In the identified parameterisation the concentration of the symmetric members is tied to the tail parameter, so the wrapped normal reached at β=2\beta = 2 is the one with σ=1/2\sigma = 1/\sqrt{2}; the skew members at β=2\beta = 2 are wrapped split normals of the matching scale.

The wrapped skew-normal of Pewsey (2000) skews the normal differently, through the factor 2Φ(αz)2\Phi(\alpha z) of Azzalini’s construction rather than through two pieces. The two families share the wrapped normal, at α=0\alpha = 0 there and at β=2\beta = 2, lam = 0.5 here:

dwsn <- function(theta, xi, omega, alpha, k = -60:60) {
  vapply(theta, function(t) {
    z <- (t + 2 * pi * k - xi) / omega
    sum(2 / omega * dnorm(z) * pnorm(alpha * z))
  }, 0)
}
rbind(wrapped_skew_normal_alpha0 = dwsn(tt, 0, sqrt(1 / 2), 0),
      wsgnstat = dwsgn(tt, mu = 0, beta = 2, lam = 0.5))
#>                                 [,1]      [,2]       [,3]
#> wrapped_skew_normal_alpha0 0.4393913 0.0103335 0.02346806
#> wsgnstat                   0.4393913 0.0103335 0.02346806

Away from the wrapped normal the two skewing mechanisms give different shapes (two half-normals joined at the mode, against a normal density reweighted by a normal distribution function), so neither family contains the other’s skew members.

Estimation from simulated data

Two estimators are provided. fit_wsgn_trig() matches the first two sample trigonometric moments to their population values (minimum distance, with sandwich standard errors); the population moments come from the characteristic function, which is evaluated through absolutely convergent integrals and is therefore available for every β>0\beta > 0, including β≤1\beta \le 1, where the Fox-Wright series representation does not converge everywhere. fit_wsgn_mle() maximises the wrapped likelihood, starting from the moment estimate; its standard errors, when asked for, come from a parametric bootstrap, because the observed information is unstable near the cusp the density develops as β\beta approaches one.

truth <- c(mu = 4, beta = 0.8, lam = 0.6)
set.seed(17)
y <- rwsgn(2000, truth["mu"], truth["beta"], truth["lam"])
ft <- fit_wsgn_trig(y)
fm <- fit_wsgn_mle(y)
round(rbind(truth = truth, moments = ft$par, moments_se = ft$se, likelihood = fm$par), 3)
#>               mu  beta   lam
#> truth      4.000 0.800 0.600
#> moments    4.202 0.809 0.723
#> moments_se 0.092 0.030 0.050
#> likelihood 4.048 0.780 0.646

The moment estimates lie within 2.5 of their own standard errors of the truth in every coordinate, and the likelihood estimates within 0.048 of it in every coordinate, at a heavy-tailed shape (β=0.8\beta = 0.8) where the characteristic function is reached only through the integral route. Bootstrap standard errors for the likelihood fit refit the model once per replicate; a small run at a lighter-tailed member:

truth2 <- c(mu = 1, beta = 1.5, lam = 0.3)
set.seed(18)
y2 <- rwsgn(500, truth2["mu"], truth2["beta"], truth2["lam"])
fb <- fit_wsgn_mle(y2, B = 30)
round(rbind(truth = truth2, estimate = fb$par, bootstrap_se = fb$se), 3)
#>                 mu  beta   lam
#> truth        1.000 1.500 0.300
#> estimate     0.957 1.459 0.289
#> bootstrap_se 0.063 0.075 0.028

An application: wind directions at Col de la Roa

The wind data in the ‘circular’ package hold 310 wind directions, in radians, recorded at a meteorological station in the Italian Alps between January and March 2001 (Agostinelli 2007). This section runs only when ‘circular’ is installed.

w <- as.numeric(wind_env$wind) %% (2 * pi)
fw_t <- fit_wsgn_trig(w)
fw <- fit_wsgn_mle(w)
round(rbind(moments = fw_t$par, moments_se = fw_t$se, likelihood = fw$par), 3)
#>                mu  beta   lam
#> moments    -0.108 2.026 0.340
#> moments_se  0.167 0.458 0.076
#> likelihood  0.026 1.355 0.322

For comparison, the wrapped normal and wrapped Cauchy laws are fitted by maximum likelihood with the ‘circular’ package, and the three fits are set side by side by log-likelihood and AIC.

wc <- circular::circular(w, type = "angles", units = "radians", template = "none",
                         modulo = "asis", zero = 0, rotation = "counter")
f_wn <- circular::mle.wrappednormal(wc)
f_wc <- circular::mle.wrappedcauchy(wc)
ll <- c(wsgn = fw$logLik,
        wrapped_normal = sum(log(circular::dwrappednormal(wc, f_wn$mu, f_wn$rho))),
        wrapped_cauchy = sum(log(circular::dwrappedcauchy(wc, f_wc$mu, f_wc$rho))))
npar <- c(3, 2, 2)
round(cbind(logLik = ll, parameters = npar, AIC = -2 * ll + 2 * npar), 1)
#>                logLik parameters   AIC
#> wsgn           -394.7          3 795.4
#> wrapped_normal -435.7          2 875.5
#> wrapped_cauchy -381.8          2 767.6
hist(w, breaks = seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 37), freq = FALSE, main = "",
     xlab = "direction (radians)")
curve(dwsgn(x, fw$par["mu"], fw$par["beta"], fw$par["lam"]), 0, 2 * pi, add = TRUE, lwd = 2)

Wind directions with the fitted wrapped skew generalised normal density.

A goodness-of-fit look uses the probability integral transform: under a correct model, pwsgn() at the fitted parameters carries the data to uniform values on (0,1)(0, 1). Kuiper’s statistic suits the circle because it does not depend on where the origin is placed. The reference distribution below ignores the estimation of the parameters, so the p-value is approximate (conservative).

u <- sort(pwsgn(w, fw$par["mu"], fw$par["beta"], fw$par["lam"]))
n <- length(u)
plot((1:n) / (n + 1), u, xlab = "uniform plotting position", ylab = "fitted distribution function",
     pch = 20, cex = 0.6, asp = 1)
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)

Probability-probability plot of the fitted model. 

V <- max((1:n) / n - u) + max(u - (0:(n - 1)) / n)
Vstar <- V * (sqrt(n) + 0.155 + 0.24 / sqrt(n))
kuiper_p <- function(v) {
  j <- 1:100
  min(1, sum(2 * (4 * j^2 * v^2 - 1) * exp(-2 * j^2 * v^2)))
}
c(V = V, V_star = Vstar, approximate_p = kuiper_p(Vstar))
#>             V        V_star approximate_p 
#>  1.970643e-01  3.502907e+00  2.114024e-09

The modified Kuiper statistic, 3.5, lies well beyond its 1 per cent critical value of 2.001 (Stephens 1970), so the fitted law is not an adequate description of these data in the absolute sense, although its AIC is 80 below that of the wrapped normal. Of the three laws compared, the smallest AIC belongs to the wrapped Cauchy law. The comparison is relative: a fit judged best among three may still be rejected, as here.

Implementation

Densities, distribution functions, quantiles, the characteristic function, the trigonometric moments and the likelihood are computed by a pure-C back-end shared with the Python package ‘wsgnstat’, which compiles the same source; the two front ends return the same values for the same inputs.

References

Agostinelli, C. (2007). Robust estimation for circular data. Computational Statistics and Data Analysis, 51(12), 5867–5875.

Pewsey, A. (2000). The wrapped skew-normal distribution on the circle. Communications in Statistics – Theory and Methods, 29(11), 2459–2472.

Stephens, M. A. (1970). Use of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Cramér-von Mises and related statistics without extensive tables. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 32(1), 115–122.
